paragraphs: Recommendation systems often have relatively few observations of which users like which items. Learning vector representations helps fill these gaps, but the paper argues that vectors struggle to express preferences involving combinations and exclusions. A request for items with two attributes but without a third requires more than a general measure of similarity.

The authors formulate recommendation as a matrix-completion problem with set relationships between rows. They represent users and attributes as boxes: multidimensional regions defined by intervals. These representations act like adjustable Venn diagrams. Their overlaps support similarity measurements using the Jaccard index, while geometric operations let the system evaluate constraints directly in the learned representation space.

The approach therefore makes the structure of a recommendation request part of the representation itself. Experiments compare box embeddings with vector-based neural methods on both simple and complex queries, reporting improvements of up to 30% overall. This is an empirical result from the evaluated recommendation settings, supporting boxes as a useful way to combine personalization with explicit set-theoretic requirements.
icml-2025-a-geometric-approach-to-person.tldr: Representing users and attributes as boxes enables personalized recommendations with explicit combinations and exclusions, with reported improvements over vector-based methods.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate outputs through a sequence of continuous, vector-valued states, with repeated evaluations of an expensive model. This paper adapts speculative sampling to accelerate that process. The basic idea is to propose candidate steps cheaply and then accept or reject them using the distribution specified by the higher-quality target model.

Speculative sampling had previously been applied to discrete sequences such as language-model tokens. Extending it to diffusion requires handling continuous Markov chains instead. The authors propose several ways to draft candidate steps, including an approach that needs no separately trained draft model and can be applied directly to an existing diffusion model.

Across the diffusion models evaluated, the method speeds generation and halves the number of function evaluations while retaining exact sampling from the target model. That combination matters because the stated acceleration preserves the target distribution rather than merely producing similar-looking outputs. The authors also show that the procedure can accelerate Langevin diffusions used to sample from unnormalized distributions, extending its use beyond generative diffusion models.
icml-2025-accelerated-diffusion-models-v.tldr: Speculative sampling accelerates continuous diffusion processes, halving function evaluations in experiments while preserving exact samples from the target model.

paragraphs: A model trained to resist one kind of adversarial attack may later encounter another. Updating it on the new attack is a natural response, but ordinary fine-tuning can weaken defenses against attacks it previously handled. The paper studies how to make this ongoing adaptation preserve earlier robustness while acquiring new protection.

Its theoretical analysis connects differences in robustness across attacks to how much each attack moves a sample in logit space, the model's internal output scores. This gives a way to reason about different attacks through their effects on the model. The authors use that connection to motivate a regularization term during training and adaptation.

Experiments cover CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNette, with more than 100 attack combinations. The proposed regularization improves robust accuracy while adding little training-time overhead. These results support logit-space regularization as a practical aid to continual robust training. The theory supplies a bound that motivates the method, while the experiments demonstrate its benefits across the tested combinations of previous and new attacks.
icml-2025-adapting-to-evolving-adversari.tldr: Regularizing attack-induced changes in model output scores helps models adapt to new adversaries while retaining robustness against earlier attacks.

paragraphs: A fixed language-model benchmark can become less informative as models and their training data change. It also gives little direct insight into how performance evolves as a model's knowledge ages. This paper proposes evaluating predictions of future events as an ongoing test of forecasting ability and generalization across time.

The authors introduce Daily Oracle, a benchmark that automatically turns daily news into question-and-answer pairs. Models are challenged to predict event outcomes, allowing evaluation to keep incorporating new material. The temporal aspect is central: it makes the age of a model's pre-training information relevant to the task being measured.

The reported findings show declining performance as pre-training data becomes outdated. Retrieval-augmented generation, which supplies retrieved information to a model, has the potential to improve prediction accuracy, but the observed degradation over time persists. The results therefore motivate continuous model updates alongside continuous evaluation. Daily Oracle contributes both a renewable source of evaluation questions and a way to observe forecasting performance as the distance from training data grows.
icml-2025-are-llms-prescient-a-continuou.tldr: Daily Oracle uses news-derived forecasting questions to track how language-model performance declines as pre-training information ages.

paragraphs: Binary classifiers can sometimes learn from differences in confidence between pairs of unlabeled examples instead of receiving a label for each example. This paper examines what supervisory information those differences contain. It identifies a particular difficulty: small confidence differences can carry noisy signals that make learning less reliable.

The authors divide the data into two subsets with different supervisory signals and construct a risk estimator with consistency regularization. This regularization encourages similar examples to receive similar outputs, reducing the influence of noisy supervision. The approach uses the structure of the available confidence information to guide how the classifier learns.

The paper also derives and analyzes estimation-error bounds, giving a theoretical account of the proposed estimator. Experiments on benchmark and UCI datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness. To investigate noise more directly, the authors artificially perturb the confidence-difference distribution and test the method under those conditions. These experiments provide evidence of robustness to the tested noise, complementing the analysis of why small confidence differences can be problematic.
icml-2025-confidence-difference-reflects.tldr: Separating confidence-difference supervision into distinct subsets and encouraging consistent predictions improves learning under the tested noisy conditions.

paragraphs: Noise in MRI measurements carries through reconstruction into the final image. Understanding that propagation helps assess reconstruction fidelity, but calculating it for deep-learning methods can be analytically and computationally difficult. This paper develops a memory-efficient way to estimate the variance at each voxel, measuring uncertainty specifically caused by acquisition noise.

The method approximates noise covariance using the reconstruction network's Jacobian, which describes how outputs change when inputs change. Explicitly calculating that object is intractable here. The authors instead derive an unbiased estimator of the diagonal of the approximated covariance matrix and implement it efficiently through Jacobian sketching. The diagonal supplies the desired voxel-level variances.

Tests use knee and brain MRI with data-driven and physics-driven networks trained under supervised and unsupervised approaches. Compared with empirical Monte Carlo references, the estimates achieve near-equivalent performance while reducing computation and memory requirements by an order of magnitude or more. Experiments also show robustness across the tested noise levels, acceleration factors, and undersampling schemes, supporting broader use of noise analysis when evaluating reconstruction methods.
icml-2025-efficient-noise-calculation-in.tldr: A Jacobian-sketching method estimates acquisition-noise variance in MRI reconstructions with substantially lower computational and memory costs than Monte Carlo references.

paragraphs: Automatic vectorization makes it convenient to run many Markov chain Monte Carlo chains together on an accelerator. However, different chains may need different amounts of work to produce a sample. In some algorithms, the parallel group must wait for the slowest chain at each iteration, creating synchronization overhead that limits the benefit of parallel execution.

The paper designs single-chain algorithms using finite state machines so that automatic vectorization avoids this overhead. This changes how the sampling procedure is organized for execution. The authors also analyze a simplified model of the process, deriving an exact expression for the speedups available within that model and using it to guide algorithm design.

They implement finite-state-machine versions of Elliptical Slice Sampling, HMC-NUTS, and Delayed Rejection. Experiments demonstrate speedups of up to an order of magnitude. The contribution connects an execution bottleneck to a concrete programming structure, with theory explaining potential gains and implementations showing that those gains can be substantial for several established sampling algorithms.
icml-2025-efficiently-vectorized-mcmc-on.tldr: Organizing MCMC algorithms as finite state machines reduces vectorization-related synchronization overhead, producing experimental speedups of up to an order of magnitude.

paragraphs: Classification models commonly learn by minimizing a tractable surrogate loss. Different losses provide different training signals, but combining them should preserve the properties that connect loss minimization to classification accuracy. EnsLoss brings ensemble learning to the choice of loss, with particular attention to maintaining convexity and calibration.

The method rewrites these requirements as conditions on loss derivatives. It can then generate calibrated derivatives directly without explicitly constructing each loss function. Inspired by Dropout, training introduces randomness in two places: the examples selected for each batch and the calibrated loss derivatives used for the update. This produces a loss ensemble within a single training process.

The authors establish statistical consistency theoretically and examine why the approach can be beneficial. Experiments demonstrate numerical effectiveness relative to fixed-loss methods across 45 pairs of CIFAR10 datasets, PCam images, and 14 OpenML tabular datasets, using several deep-learning architectures. The contribution is a way to vary the learning objective during training while retaining theoretical support for its connection to accurate classification.
icml-2025-ensloss-stochastic-calibrated-.tldr: EnsLoss randomly combines calibrated loss derivatives during one training run, preserving statistical consistency and showing benefits over fixed-loss methods.

paragraphs: An individual report of harm can be meaningful evidence, but understanding whether it reflects a broader disparity requires aggregating reports. This paper studies a reporting database in which adverse-event reports arrive over time. The goal is to identify subgroups, defined by combinations of relevant features, that experience disproportionately high rates of harmful interactions.

The authors formulate this as sequential hypothesis testing, allowing evidence to accumulate as reports arrive. They identify conditions on reporting behavior that are sufficient to support inferences about underlying harm rates. This distinction matters because the frequency of submitted reports is not automatically the same as the frequency of actual harm.

Under the stated reporting conditions, existing sequential-testing algorithms can be used with a standard correction for testing multiple hypotheses. Demonstrations on mortgage decisions and vaccine side effects recover subgroups already known to experience disproportionate harm, using only a fraction of the data originally used to discover them. The results show how incoming reports can support earlier identification of disparities when the reporting process permits those inferences.
icml-2025-from-individual-experience-to-.tldr: A sequential-testing framework turns accumulating harm reports into evidence of subgroup disparities under sufficient conditions on reporting behavior.

paragraphs: Discovering causal structure is difficult when some relevant variables are hidden, and selection bias adds another complication. The observed sample can have a different joint distribution from the population of interest. This paper investigates whether covariance information can still reveal causal structure when latent variables and selection bias occur together.

The analysis focuses on linear Gaussian models and rank constraints on covariance submatrices. These constraints generalize information provided by conditional independence. The authors show that selection can substantially change the distribution while leaving matrix ranks informative about both the causal graph and the selection mechanism. They provide a graph-based characterization of those surviving constraints.

Using this characterization, the paper demonstrates that a one-factor latent-variable model can be identified under selection bias. Simulations and real-world experiments support the effectiveness of the proposed rank constraints. The contribution is a statistical tool for a setting where standard latent-variable methods have lacked an adaptation to selection, together with a concrete identification result showing what that tool can recover.
icml-2025-latent-variable-causal-discove.tldr: Covariance rank constraints retain useful causal information under selection bias and enable identification of a one-factor model in the studied setting.

paragraphs: This paper studies how many observations are needed to recover the graph of a directed Gaussian model under an equal-variance assumption. Earlier sample bounds depend on the number of nodes and maximum in-degree, but also grow polynomially with the covariance matrix's condition number. That additional dependence can make the requirements large in high-dimensional problems.

The authors give a graph-recovery algorithm whose required sample count is independent of the condition number. They also establish lower bounds that nearly match the upper bound, with a remaining factor involving the maximum in-degree. Together, these results clarify how much data the problem intrinsically requires without imposing a condition-number bound.

The paper separately addresses computational efficiency. With an additional assumption that all variable variances are bounded, it provides a polynomial-time recovery algorithm at the price of extra polynomial sample dependence on the maximum in-degree. Synthetic-data simulations confirm the theoretical predictions. The distinction matters: the strongest sample result and the efficient algorithm come with different stated requirements and costs.
icml-2025-learning-gaussian-dag-models-w.tldr: Under equal variances, Gaussian graph recovery can avoid condition-number-dependent sample requirements, with an efficient algorithm available under an additional bounded-variance assumption.

paragraphs: Good prediction performance across an entire population can conceal weaker performance within subgroups. This paper defines relevant subpopulations through the components of a mixture model. It considers two ways to assign people to those components: choosing the most likely component, or distributing membership across components according to their relative likelihoods.

Using online calibration as its case study, the paper develops a multi-objective algorithm that handles all plausible underlying subgroup structures simultaneously. This avoids first committing to one recovered clustering. The method provides subgroup guarantees under both membership definitions and achieves an O(T^(1/2)) rate even when the components are not well separated.

The comparison is a cluster-then-predict approach, which has an O(T^(2/3)) rate and requires separable subpopulations. The theoretical result shows that obtaining calibrated predictions within underlying groups can be easier than identifying those groups themselves. In particular, the studied cluster-learning problem requires separation between median subgroup features, whereas the subgroup-calibration guarantees do not. This separates the need for reliable subgroup performance from the need to reconstruct subgroup membership.
icml-2025-learning-with-multi-group-guar.tldr: An online calibration algorithm guarantees performance across mixture-model subgroups without requiring the separation needed to learn the clusters themselves.

paragraphs: Temporal graph neural networks process graphs whose nodes and connections evolve over time. Many attacks assume access to the complete input graph, but an attacker may only know the graph as it currently exists. This paper studies vulnerabilities under that restriction, where future changes can otherwise weaken an attack or place new nodes beyond its immediate reach.

MemFreezing injects fake nodes or edges to push node memories into a stable state that responds weakly to later graph changes. Because these memories become less responsive, they convey less useful information. The proposed mechanism also lets affected nodes maintain and spread this frozen state through neighboring nodes as the graph continues evolving.

Experiments show persistent performance degradation across several temporal-graph tasks without requiring knowledge of the graph after the attack. The contribution is therefore an attack framework aimed at both lasting and spreading disruption under limited future knowledge. It identifies node-memory dynamics as a source of vulnerability that can remain relevant even when the attacker cannot anticipate later graph events.
icml-2025-memfreezing-a-novel-adversaria.tldr: MemFreezing disrupts temporal graph networks by making node memories persistently unresponsive, without requiring knowledge of future graph changes.

paragraphs: Visual brain decoding aims to reconstruct what a person sees from fMRI signals. Differences between people's brains make models trained on one person difficult to reuse for another, while limited fMRI data makes separate training costly. MindAligner addresses this transfer problem by explicitly aligning brain function across subjects.

Its central component is a learned Brain Transfer Matrix that maps a new subject's signals into the signal space of a known subject. This allows an already trained decoding model to be reused. A Brain Functional Alignment module supports learning that mapping through soft alignment across subjects exposed to different visual stimuli and a loss that checks alignment at multiple levels.

Experiments report better visual decoding than existing methods when data is limited. The alignment also reveals fine-grained functional correspondences, which the authors describe as interpretable and useful for cross-subject neuroscience analysis. The approach therefore combines a practical transfer mechanism with an explicit representation of how subjects correspond, addressing both reuse of decoding models and investigation of functional similarities between brains.
icml-2025-mindaligner-explicit-brain-fun.tldr: MindAligner maps a new subject's fMRI signals to a known subject's representation, improving visual decoding with limited data and exposing functional correspondences.

paragraphs: Planning in highly stochastic or partially observable environments involves uncertainty about the values of possible decisions. This paper develops a Monte Carlo Tree Search backup rule that carries that uncertainty through the search tree. Both value nodes and action-value nodes are represented as Gaussian distributions instead of only single numerical estimates.

The backup operation combines child action-value distributions using a Wasserstein barycenter, a distributional form of averaging based on optimal transport. This propagates uncertainty toward the root, where the overall decision is made. The authors study a combination of an L1-Wasserstein barycenter and alpha-divergence, establishing a connection to generalized-mean backup operators.

They pair the probabilistic backup with sampling strategies based on optimistic selection and Thompson sampling to form Wasserstein MCTS. The paper gives asymptotic convergence guarantees toward the optimal policy at O(n^(-1/2)), where n counts visited trajectories. Experiments in several stochastic and partially observable environments outperform related baselines. Together, the results support treating uncertainty propagation as an explicit part of tree search.
icml-2025-monte-carlo-tree-search-with-u.tldr: Wasserstein MCTS propagates Gaussian value uncertainty through optimal-transport backups, with convergence guarantees and improved results in tested uncertain environments.

paragraphs: Online knapsack algorithms must make selection decisions as items arrive, without the complete information available to an offline solution. Predictions can help guide those decisions, but trusting them introduces a trade-off. Consistency captures the benefit of useful predictions, while robustness concerns performance when predictions are unreliable. This paper develops algorithms that balance those objectives.

The proposed family combines a trusted learning-augmented algorithm with an algorithm designed for worst-case performance. Its predictions are compact: a single value or an interval estimating the minimum item value in an offline solution. This gives the method a specific, succinct piece of predictive information to use when making online decisions.

The authors establish near Pareto-optimal consistency-robustness trade-offs, meaning the resulting balance is close to the frontier of what can be jointly achieved. They also introduce a procedure for converting fractional solutions into integral ones. That conversion contributes to the design of online algorithms that must ultimately make discrete selections, while the main result shows how combining predictive and worst-case methods can approach the attainable trade-off.
icml-2025-near-optimal-consistency-robus.tldr: Combining prediction-guided and worst-case algorithms yields near-optimal trade-offs between consistency and robustness for online knapsack problems.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo Tree Search plans by using simulations to estimate the consequences of decisions. In real-world applications, the simulator may not accurately represent how the environment changes or what rewards it produces. This paper introduces a robust version of tree search that explicitly addresses ambiguity in both transition dynamics and reward distributions.

The method combines a robust power-mean backup operator with carefully chosen exploration bonuses. The backup controls how information from explored branches is combined, while exploration bonuses guide where additional simulations are spent. The design supports finite-sample convergence guarantees at every node, connecting local tree-search updates to the reliability of the overall value estimate.

For the root node, the authors establish an O(n^(-1/2)) convergence rate, comparable to standard MCTS. Experiments also provide evidence of robust planning performance under substantial ambiguity in rewards and transitions. The contribution is a planning algorithm that accounts for model mismatch while retaining the stated convergence rate, supported by empirical tests of the ambiguity it is designed to handle.
icml-2025-online-robust-reinforcement-le.tldr: A robust MCTS variant handles uncertainty in simulator dynamics and rewards while achieving a root-value convergence rate comparable to standard MCTS.

paragraphs: Graph clustering often looks for groups with relatively few connections leading outside them, an objective associated with low conductance. This paper follows a different emphasis: connections between groups can themselves be important for understanding a graph. It studies bipartite-like clusters, bringing that interconnection structure into the clustering problem.

The authors present efficient online algorithms for finding these clusters in both undirected and directed graphs. Covering both settings matters because the methods address graphs where connections are symmetric as well as graphs where their direction carries information. The work links the search for bipartite-like structure to the computational challenge of analyzing massive graphs.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that the proposed algorithms substantially accelerate existing clustering algorithms while preserving their effectiveness. The stated benefit therefore combines faster execution with maintained clustering performance in the evaluated settings. More broadly, the paper contributes methods for studying relationships between clusters, expanding the kinds of graph organization that efficient clustering procedures can usefully expose.
icml-2025-online-sparsification-of-bipar.tldr: Online algorithms find bipartite-like clusters in directed and undirected graphs, accelerating tested clustering methods while preserving their effectiveness.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient learning can require many samples because its gradient estimates have high variance. This paper introduces SoftTreeMax, which incorporates planning into the softmax mechanism used to select actions. It extends the model's current scores with discounted rewards accumulated over multiple future steps and scores evaluated at the resulting future states.

The analysis explains how expanding a planning tree can reduce gradient variance. The amount of reduction depends on the policy used to expand the tree: stronger decay occurs when the induced transitions are closer to being independent of the current state. For approximate forward models, the authors also bound gradient bias, showing that it diminishes with model approximation error while the variance reduction remains.

A practical implementation uses a parallel GPU simulator to expand trees efficiently. In Atari experiments, SoftTreeMax reduces gradient variance by three orders of magnitude and achieves better sample complexity and performance than distributed PPO. These findings connect the theoretical variance analysis to an implementation where looking ahead improves the learning signal.
icml-2025-policy-gradient-with-tree-expa.tldr: SoftTreeMax adds tree-based planning to policy gradients, reducing variance with theoretical guarantees and improving Atari results over distributed PPO.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo Tree Search becomes harder to analyze when actions and states are continuous and outcomes are stochastic. Existing approaches combine tree search with hierarchical exploration, but the paper identifies a gap in convergence guarantees for this setting. In particular, guarantees developed for deterministic environments do not supply the corresponding stochastic theory.

The proposed Stochastic-Power-HOOT algorithm combines a power-mean value backup with a polynomial exploration bonus. The backup determines how values from explored branches are aggregated. The exploration bonus addresses the non-stationarity that arises in continuous-action search, where the estimation problem changes as exploration proceeds. These components are designed together for continuous, stochastic Markov decision processes.

The authors establish a non-asymptotic polynomial convergence rate of O(n^(-zeta)), with zeta between zero and one-half and n denoting visited trajectories. This extends the type of convergence guarantee provided by POLY-HOOT to stochastic environments. Experiments on stochastic tasks support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the proposed algorithm's effectiveness in the continuous, uncertain domains it targets.
icml-2025-power-mean-estimation-in-stoch.tldr: Stochastic-Power-HOOT combines power-mean backups and polynomial exploration bonuses to obtain convergence guarantees for continuous, stochastic tree search.

paragraphs: A model trained on incorrect labels can sometimes improve when trained again using its own definite class predictions as labels. This paper provides a theoretical explanation in a specific setting: linearly separable binary classification with randomly corrupted labels. Under that setup, the authors prove that retraining can improve population accuracy over the initial noisy-label training.

The paper also studies an application to local label differential privacy, where label noise is part of the training setup. It introduces consensus-based retraining, which selects examples whose predicted labels agree with their supplied labels. This agreement rule determines which examples participate in the second training stage.

Empirically, consensus-based retraining improves label-private training without additional privacy cost. For ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 at epsilon equal to three, the authors report an accuracy improvement exceeding 6%. The theoretical and empirical contributions address related but distinct claims: retraining can help under the analyzed binary-classification assumptions, and selecting agreeing examples produces substantial gains in the reported private-training experiment.
icml-2025-retraining-with-predicted-hard.tldr: Retraining on predicted hard labels can improve accuracy under stated noisy-label assumptions, while consensus-based retraining improves tested label-private training without extra privacy cost.

paragraphs: Face-swapping systems can enable unauthorized manipulation of protected individuals and make generated images difficult to trace. Secure Swap addresses these concerns inside the face-swapping model. It distinguishes designated persons of interest from other subjects, applying protection to the former and provenance marking to outputs involving the latter.

An ID Passport layer redacts faces belonging to persons of interest. For other subjects, the system produces swapped images containing a unique invisible watermark. A detachable watermark encoder and decoder are trained with the model, allowing outputs to carry information that can later be extracted for provenance tracing.

The experiments report a 100% protection success rate for persons of interest and more than 99% watermark extraction accuracy for other subjects, while preserving face-swap functionality. They also demonstrate robustness against image-level and model-level attacks in online and offline scenarios. These are experimental outcomes in the evaluated settings, supporting a design that combines restrictions on selected identities with traceability of permitted face-swapping outputs.
icml-2025-robust-secure-swap-responsible.tldr: Secure Swap combines protection for designated identities with invisible provenance watermarks, achieving high protection and extraction rates in experiments.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts pretrained models through restricted parameter changes. This paper draws a connection between the low-rank structure of those changes and biological ideas about neural engrams and long-term synaptic development. That connection motivates Synapse and Neuron, or SAN, a method for organizing how fine-tuning adjustments propagate through a model.

SAN decomposes the scaling component of earlier feature-adjustment vectors and propagates it toward later weight matrices. The authors ground this design in long-term potentiation and depression, biological phenomena associated with changes in synapses. The biological framing supplies a proposed rationale for the adaptation mechanism; the reported performance evidence comes from machine-learning tasks.

On vision tasks across 25 datasets, SAN exceeds full fine-tuning by up to 8.7% and LoRA by 3.2%. On eight commonsense-reasoning datasets with LLaMA models, reported gains reach 8.5% over ChatGPT and 4.7% over LoRA. On seven visual-instruction-tuning datasets with LLaVA, it exceeds full fine-tuning by up to 2.4% and LoRA by 1.9%. These results support its effectiveness across the evaluated modalities and architectures.
icml-2025-san-hypothesizing-long-term-sy.tldr: SAN uses a biologically motivated redistribution of scaling adjustments for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, with reported gains across vision, language, and vision-language tasks.

paragraphs: Traditional autoregressive forecasting uses discrete time lags to relate past observations to future values. This paper instead learns a continuous time-shift operator: a mapping from a system's history up to a given time to its later values. The formulation covers both temporal data and data that varies across space and time.

The authors represent this mapping with Khatri-Rao neural operators, a proposed architecture built from non-stationary integral transforms. The architecture has nearly linear computational scaling. Its continuous formulation naturally accommodates observations collected at irregular intervals and supports forecasts at finer spatial and temporal resolution, connecting flexible observation times with flexible prediction locations.

Numerical studies across diverse temporal and spatio-temporal benchmarks report performance that is either state of the art or competitive with leading methods. The contribution is therefore both a forecasting formulation and an architecture for implementing it efficiently. The stated results support the framework across the evaluated benchmarks, while its continuous operator structure supplies the mechanism for handling irregular sampling and forecasting at super-resolution.
icml-2025-shifting-time-time-series-fore.tldr: Khatri-Rao neural operators learn a continuous time-shift mapping that supports irregular observations and finer-resolution forecasting with competitive benchmark performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies correlation clustering in a graph that grows one node at a time. The algorithm accesses graph information through database queries and updates its clustering after each insertion. The central challenge is to maintain a useful clustering while keeping the computational cost of repeated updates small as the graph becomes larger.

The proposed Sparse-pivot algorithm achieves an amortized update time of log raised to a constant power of n. Amortized time describes the cost averaged over a sequence of updates, rather than a guarantee that every individual insertion takes the same amount of work. Its approximation factor is 20 plus epsilon, substantially improving the guarantee of the prior algorithm in this insertion model.

The authors also evaluate the algorithm empirically and report better performance than that earlier method. The contribution combines a stronger theoretical clustering guarantee with inexpensive updates and supporting practical results. It directly addresses a setting where the graph and its clustering must be maintained together as new nodes arrive through an ongoing sequence of insertions.
icml-2025-sparse-pivot-dynamic-correlati.tldr: Sparse-pivot improves the approximation guarantee for node-insertion correlation clustering while retaining polylogarithmic amortized update time.
